Theme: Screening Scales in Psychiatry — Indications and Cut-Offs

Match each scale to its PRIMARY PURPOSE:

A. PHQ-9
B. GAD-7
C. AUDIT
D. CAGE
E. HCL-32
F. MDQ
G. PANSS
H. Y-BOCS
I. HAM-D
J. MADRS
K. MMSE
L. MoCA
M. ACE-III
N. HCR-20
options: A 10-item screening questionnaire for alcohol use disorders developed by the WHO. Scores of 8+ indicate hazardous drinking; 16+ harmful; 20+ possible dependence.

A 4-item screening tool for ALCOHOL DEPENDENCE (not hazardous drinking). Two or more YES answers indicates possible alcohol dependence. It asks about C utting down, A nnoyance by criticism, G uilt, and E ye-openers.
A 15-item clinician-administered scale for NEGATIVE SYMPTOMS of schizophrenia — assesses blunted affect, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, asociality.
A 32-item self-report screening tool for BIPOLAR SPECTRUM disorders, designed to detect hypomanic symptoms. Cut-off of ≥14 indicates possible bipolarity.
distractors_rationale: AUDIT (C) — Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test. Developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) for international use. 10 items (8 questions + 2 about consequences). Score ranges from 0-40. INTERPRETATION: 0-7 = Low risk; 8-15 = Hazardous drinking; 16-19 = Harmful drinking; 20+ = Possible alcohol dependence. AUDIT is more comprehensive than CAGE and is the recommended screening tool by NICE CG115. AUDIT-C (first 3 items: frequency, quantity, binge drinking) is an abbreviated version used in primary care (cut-off ≥5 for men, ≥4 for women indicates hazardous drinking).

CAGE (D). A brief (4-item) screening tool for ALCOHOL DEPENDENCE. Questions: (1) Have you ever felt you should CUT DOWN on your drinking? (2) Have people ANNOYED you by criticising your drinking? (3) Have you ever felt GUILTY about your drinking? (4) Have you ever had an EYE-OPENER (a drink first thing in the morning) to steady your nerves or get rid of a hangover? SCORING: ≥2 = 'positive' for possible alcohol dependence (sensitivity 85%, specificity 78% for dependence). LIMITATION: CAGE asks about LIFETIME symptoms (not current) — it may miss current hazardous drinking patterns in young people. CAGE does not assess AMOUNT of alcohol consumed. NICE recommends AUDIT over CAGE for screening. The CAGE is still commonly asked about in the MRCPsych exam.

This is the SANS — Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (Andreasen, 1982). Negative symptoms of schizophrenia: the '5 A's: ALOOGIA (poverty of speech), ANHEDONIA (loss of pleasure), A VOLITION (loss of motivation), A SOCIALITY (social withdrawal), AFFECTIVE BLUNTING. PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale) assesses both positive AND negative symptoms plus general psychopathology. The SANS/SAPS (Scale for Assessment of Positive Symptoms) are research scales rather than routine clinical tools. The BPRS (Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale) is a 18-24 item clinician-rated scale for general psychopathology.

HCL-32 (E) — Hypomania Checklist (Angst et al., 2005). A 32-item self-report tool designed to DETECT LIFETIME HYPOMANIC SYMPTOMS, specifically for use in patients presenting with depression to screen for BIPOLAR II. Cut-off: ≥14 items endorsed = positive screen (sensitivity 80%, specificity 51%). The HCL-32 is more sensitive than the MDQ for bipolar II (the MDQ was designed primarily for bipolar I). The MDQ (Mood Disorder Questionnaire): 13 items, cut-off ≥7. The MDQ has better specificity but lower sensitivity than the HCL-32 for bipolar II. For MRCPsych: know that HCL-32 is preferred for screening in DEPRESSED patients to detect bipolar II; MDQ is better for screening in the general population for bipolar I.
teaching_point: Screening scales — HIGH-YIELD for MRCPsych EMI questions: DEPRESSION: PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire) — 9 items, cut-off ≥10 for MDD. HAM-D/HDRS (Hamilton Depression Rating Scale) — 17-item, clinician-rated, cut-off 7-17 mild, 18-24 moderate, >24 severe. MADRS (Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale) — 10-item, more sensitive to change than HAM-D. BDI (Beck Depression Inventory-II) — 21 items, self-report. GDS-15 (Geriatric Depression Scale) — for elderly. ALCOHOL: AUDIT (10 items, cut-off ≥8), CAGE (4 items, cut-off ≥2), SADQ (Severity of Alcohol Dependence). ANXIETY: GAD-7 (7 items, cut-off ≥8). COGNITION: MMSE (30 points, cut-off <24 suggests dementia), MoCA (30 points, cut-off <26 suggests MCI), ACE-III (100 points, cut-off <88 MCI, <82 dementia). PSYCHOSIS: PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale), BPRS (Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale). BIPOLAR: HCL-32 (≥14), MDQ (≥7). OCD: Y-BOCS (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale) — 10 items, 0-40. VIOLENCE RISK: HCR-20. PSYCHOPATHY: PCL-R.
source: WHO AUDIT guidelines; Ewing JA (1984) CAGE; Angst J et al. (2005) HCL-32; NICE guidelines

stem: A 48-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia (paranoid subtype, well-controlled on paliperidone LAI 100mg monthly for 5 years) is referred to a bariatric clinic for weight loss surgery. Her current BMI is 42. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and obstructive sleep apnoea. She has been stable with no psychiatric admissions for 4 years. She is seeking a gastric bypass. Her psychiatrist has been informed about the referral. Which of the following is TRUE regarding bariatric surgery in patients with severe mental illness?
options: Schizophrenia is an absolute contraindication to bariatric surgery — the risk of non-adherence and psychiatric decompensation is too high

Bariatric surgery in stable schizophrenia is safe and effective when: pre-operative psychiatric clearance is given, medication levels are monitored, and a multi-disciplinary team supports the patient post-operatively
She must be switched from paliperidone LAI to oral antipsychotic before surgery
Weight loss surgery will not affect her antipsychotic absorption
Paliperidone LAI cannot be used in patients with diabetes
distractors_rationale: Stable schizophrenia is NOT an absolute contraindication to bariatric surgery. The NICE guideline on obesity (NG189) and the psychiatric evaluation for bariatric surgery emphasise that severe mental illness is not an exclusion criterion WHEN it is STABLE and the patient has good insight and support.

CORRECT. Bariatric surgery in stable schizophrenia is safe and effective WHEN: (1) PRE-OPERATIVE PSYCHIATRIC CLEARANCE — by a psychiatrist familiar with the patient, confirming stability (no acute psychosis, stable medication, good adherence, insight, social support, realistic expectations); (2) ANTIPSYCHOTIC MONITORING — post-operatively, weight loss, changes in absorption (especially with gastric bypass/malabsorptive procedures), and changes in renal function can affect antipsychotic levels. Bariatric surgery can ALTER the absorption of oral medication due to anatomical changes (gastric bypass → reduced stomach acid → altered tablet dissolution). LAI (paliperidone) is NOT absorbed orally so its pharmacokinetics are NOT affected by bariatric surgery — it is the IDEAL formulation in this patient, as oral antipsychotic absorption may be unpredictable after gastric bypass. (3) MULTIDISIPLINARY TEAM — including psychiatry, bariatric surgery, dietetics, and endocrinology. (4) MONITORING: (a) Antipsychotic levels after surgery; (b) Psychiatric status (stress of surgery can trigger relapse); (c) Weight and metabolic outcomes. The patient should be assessed by the bariatric MDT with input from her CMHT/psychiatrist.

She does NOT need to switch from LAI — the LAI is actually PREFERABLE because its absorption is not affected by bariatric surgery (IM injection is independent of gastrointestinal function). Oral medication absorption may be unpredictable after gastric bypass. If she were on ORAL antipsychotic, she would need monitoring of levels post-operatively and may need dose adjustment (or switch to LAI). LAI is the safest option.

Bariatric surgery CAN affect oral medication absorption. Gastric bypass: reduced stomach size and altered anatomy can affect the absorption of many oral medications, including antipsychotics. LAI formulations are not affected.
Paliperidone can cause weight gain and metabolic side effects (less than olanzapine/clozapine) but is NOT contraindicated in diabetes.
teaching_point: Bariatric surgery in severe mental illness — principles for MRCPsych: (1) Severe mental illness (schizophrenia, bipolar, depression) is NOT a contraindication to bariatric surgery if it is STABLE. (2) PSYCHIATRIC EVALUATION is a standard part of the pre-operative assessment for all bariatric patients (not just those with known mental illness). (3) Factors associated with POOR post-operative outcomes: UNSTABLE psychiatric illness, poor adherence to treatment, substance misuse, eating disorder (binge eating disorder, bulimia), poor social support, unrealistic expectations. (4) ANTIPSYCHOTIC MANAGEMENT: PREFER LAIs (no absorption issues). For oral antipsychotics: monitor levels post-operatively; consider dose adjustment; avoid extended-release formulations if absorption is unpredictable. (5) Psychiatric monitoring: the peri-operative period is stressful and may trigger relapse — close follow-up by CMHT is essential. (6) OUTCOMES: studies show that stable schizophrenia patients who undergo bariatric surgery have SIMILAR weight loss outcomes to the general population. The surgery can also improve diabetes, hypertension, sleep apnoea — which are common in patients on antipsychotics.
source: NICE NG189: Obesity; NICE CG178; Sarwer DB et al. (2016) Bariatric surgery in SMI; BNF

stem: A 30-year-old man with known epilepsy (generalised tonic-clonic seizures, well-controlled on lamotrigine 200mg daily) is brought to A&E after being found wandering and confused. He is on no other medications. He has a 2-day history of fever (38.2°C), headache, and neck stiffness. On examination: photophobia, neck stiffness, and a non-blanching petechial rash over his trunk. He is confused (GCS 14). He is started on IV antibiotics for suspected bacterial meningitis. Two days later, he becomes increasingly agitated, disoriented, and develops new-onset generalised tonic-clonic seizures. What is the MOST LIKELY cause of his deterioration?
options: The meningitis has caused a subdural empyema requiring neurosurgery
He is developing lamotrigine toxicity (due to the infection and fever reducing the seizure threshold and possibly affecting lamotrigine metabolism)
He has developed anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis secondary to the infection
Delirium due to the infection — treat with haloperidol
He has developed status epilepticus due to the meningitis
distractors_rationale: Subdural empyema is a complication of bacterial meningitis but would require CT/MRI to diagnose. The description of new seizures and confusion could also be explained by lamotrigine toxicity.

CORRECT. Lamotrigine is an antiepileptic that carries a risk of SEVERE ADVERSE DRUG REACTIONS including: (1) STEVENS-JOHNSON SYNDROME (SJS) / TOXIC EPIDERMAL NECROLYSIS (TEN) — the most feared side effect, presenting with fever, rash (petechial → blistering → skin sloughing), and mucosal involvement. However, this patient already has a petechial rash from MENINGOCOCCAL DISEASE, which confuses the picture. (2) RISK FACTORS FOR LAMOTRIGINE TOXICITY: (a) RAPID dose titration (the main risk — must be slow: 25mg for 2 weeks, then 50mg, then 100mg, then 200mg); (b) COMBINATION with valproate (increases lamotrigine levels by 2-3×) — not relevant here; (c) INFECTION/ FEVER — can affect drug metabolism and lower the seizure threshold; (d) RENAL/HEPATIC IMPAIRMENT; (e) INTERACTIONS — oral contraceptives reduce lamotrigine levels; (f) This patient has fever + infection (meningitis) + new seizures → possible lamotrigine toxicity. However, the petechial rash is more likely due to the meningococcal sepsis itself (meningococcaemia) rather than SJS (which presents with more widespread, blistering rash typically starting on the face and upper trunk 1-8 weeks after starting lamotrigine). The seizures could also be due to the MENINGITIS itself (meningoencephalitis). The most LIKELY explanation: the patient's lamotrigine metabolism has been affected by the infection (fever, systemic inflammation), reducing his seizure threshold and possibly causing lamotrigine accumulation. PLUS the meningitis itself is causing cerebral irritation. The management: (1) Check lamotrigine level; (2) If toxic → reduce/stop; (3) Consider an alternative antiepileptic (levetiracetam) for seizure control; (4) CT head to exclude empyema/ abscess.

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis can be triggered by infection (herpes simplex encephalitis) but is not typically triggered by bacterial meningitis. The diagnosis would be suggested by: CSF pleocytosis, anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, and movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesia).
Delirium is part of the picture but the worsening seizure activity requires a more specific explanation.
Status epilepticus (continuous seizure >5 minutes) is a possible complication of meningitis but the description suggests a relapse of seizures, not continuous activity.
teaching_point: Lamotrigine side effects — HIGH-YIELD for MRCPsych: (1) SJS/TEN: incidence ~0.1% with SLOW titration; up to 1% with FAST titration. MEDICAL EMERGENCY. Presents with: fever, rash (target lesions, blistering), mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital), skin sloughing. Management: STOP lamotrigine IMMEDIATELY, hospital admission, dermatology review. (2) SJS is hard to distinguish from VIRAL RASH/INFECTION — any new rash in the first 2-8 weeks of lamotrigine should be taken seriously. (3) LAMOTRIGINE AND VALPROATE: valproate DOUBLES lamotrigine levels → slower titration required (max 25mg every 2 weeks for the first 2 months). (4) LAMOTRIGINE AND PREGNANCY: levels DROP by 50% in pregnancy (increased clearance) → increase dose. Levels RISE postpartum → reduce dose within 48h to avoid toxicity. (5) Oral contraceptives reduce lamotrigine levels by 50% → may need dose adjustment. (6) Risk of SUICIDALITY: all antiepileptics carry a small increased risk. (7) Lamotrigine is the ONLY mood stabiliser that is NOT a teratogen — it is the safest option in pregnancy for bipolar maintenance. (8) For seizure control: lamotrigine is broad-spectrum (generalised and focal seizures). Other antiepileptics to know: valproate (broad spectrum, teratogenic), carbamazepine (focal seizures, CYP450 inducer, hyponatraemia), levetiracetam (newer, broad spectrum, well-tolerated, behavioural side effects), phenytoin (narrow therapeutic index, enzyme-inducing).
source: BNF; NICE CG185: Bipolar; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines; Rzany B et al. (1999) Lamotrigine and SJS
